findings.problem: The "True" explanation says "Remember my phone charger? Like that, but on purpose." The setup in the Prep story card (stop 2, card 3) was the baker's charger: "somebody walking off with your phone charger and you NEVER sending the 'hey, you still got my charger?' text." It was never Papa Dorin's charger, so the callback points to a setup that didn't happen. It also gives Papa Dorin a phone charger, which is new to his world.

rule.text: A callback only works if its setup came earlier in this lesson or conversation.

findings.problem: The "True" explanation says "Somebody cuts me off in traffic and my mustache is waving." Papa Dorin lives on a cookie planet just big enough for his bakery, so him driving in traffic adds something new to his world. Everyday adult life is fine for comparisons with the baker, but not as his own experience.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The "To hear Him and to be healed" explanation opens with "Ears open and hearts hurting, that's the crowd." Luke 6:18 says they came to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases. It says nothing about their hearts hurting. That's a feeling stated as fact.

rule.text: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

findings.problem: The "humble" explanation says "That's the Father the listeners are called to look like, right in the same verse where they're called sons of the Most High (Luke 6:35)." Luke 6:35 says "you will be sons of the Most High," a promised result, not a name they're called now. And Luke 6:35 says "the Most High," not "the Father"; "your Father" comes in Luke 6:36. Keep the text's own words and verse.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Most explanations follow the same pattern: the answer echoed back with "baker" or "friend" ("LEAP, baker!" 1/10, "Your tunic, baker!" 2/2, "Ungrateful, baker!" 2/10, "Into a pit, baker!" 3/2, "A BEAM, friend!" 3/6, "Fruit, friend!" 3/11, "The mouth, baker!" 3/13, "True!" 1/18, 2/8, 3/9, "True, friend." 2/6, 3/4), then "Jesus says, '...' (Luke 6:N)," then a short joke. Nearly every one of the 72 explanations uses "Jesus says" plus a quote. Taken together this reads as a formula. Vary the openers and how the verse comes in.

rule.text: There is no formula. Each explanation sounds natural and different from the others.

findings.problem: Two jokes have Papa Dorin sulking: "Somebody calls my stamps crooked and I sulk for a week" (1/10 Rejoice) and "if somebody skipped the thank you on one cookie, I'd be sulking by the oven for an hour" (2/10 ungrateful). In the same lesson he says "I don't hold grudges, friend" (2/12 forgiven). papa-dorin.md wants self-deprecating humor but also says he never holds a grudge and his humor reflects kindness and forgiveness.
findings.question: Is self-deprecating humor about sulking or staying upset fine for Papa Dorin, or does it clash with "He never holds a grudge"?

findings.problem: Some right-answer explanations open with praise that works like a reaction: "False, and nice catch!" (1/13), "False, and you caught it!" (3/16), "You got it." (1/6), "That's the one, friend." (2/4), "That's it, baker." (3/18). The code already shows a right-answer reaction first. These phrases aren't in the reaction list, so the rule doesn't clearly cover them.
findings.question: Does "The explanation never includes a reaction" mean only the listed reaction phrases, or any praise opener like "nice catch!" and "You got it"?

findings.problem: The "You brood of vipers" explanation says "Those words come from John the Baptist, friend" (Luke 3:7). That's true in Luke, but Jesus Himself says "brood of vipers" in Matthew 12:34 and 23:33. A baker who knows Matthew may read this as saying Jesus never used the phrase.
findings.question: When a wrong answer points to another passage, should Papa Dorin stick to the same book (here Luke), or must the claim hold for the whole Bible?

findings.problem: The "old" explanation says "The question is true or false." On a fill-in-the-blank card this reads as if the card were a true/false question. It means the contrast is true versus false prophets, but the passage never says "true prophets" (Luke 6:23 just says "the prophets"). The "false" explanation also calls them "the real prophets."
findings.question: Is this wordplay clear enough, and is "real/true prophets" an acceptable way to name "the prophets" of Luke 6:23?
